stops.name: Piandarca, between Cannara and Bevagna, the sermon to the birds
stops.campa: On the plain called Piandarca, walking from Cannara toward Bevagna, Francesco lifts his eyes and sees the trees by the road filled with birds beyond counting. 'Wait for me here,' he tells his companions, 'while I go and preach to my sisters the birds.' He walks in among them; not one flies. He preaches; they stretch their necks, spread their wings, open their beaks, and touch his tunic with their heads. He signs them with the cross and they rise singing into the four quarters of the sky. From that day he calls all creatures brother and sister.
stops.quote: My brother birds, you ought greatly to praise your Creator and love Him always: He gave you feathers to wear, wings to fly, and whatever you need. God made you noble among His creatures and gave you a home in the purity of the air; you neither sow nor reap, and yet He protects and governs you without any care of your own.
stops.quote_source: Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima 58; Fioretti 16

stops.name: Porziuncola, Clare's flight and tonsure
stops.campa: Palm Sunday night. Chiara di Favarone, eighteen, noble, leaves her father's palace by the door of the dead, the low door used only for corpses, and comes down through the olive groves to the torchlit Porziuncola, where the brothers wait with lamps. Before the altar of Saint Mary, Francesco cuts off her golden hair and clothes her in sackcloth and the veil: the Order of Poor Ladies begins. He shelters her with the nuns of San Paolo at Bastia, where her armed kinsmen fail to tear her from the altar cloths; soon she is set at San Damiano, as he prophesied while begging its stones.

stops.name: Alviano, the silencing of the swallows
stops.campa: At Alviano above the Tiber the whole town gathers to hear him, but the swallows nesting in the eaves are shrieking so that no one can hear a word. Francesco addresses them as he addresses everyone. The swallows fall silent at once and do not stir until the sermon is done. The people, Celano says, were amazed and gave glory to God; the fame of it runs through the valley faster than any bird.
stops.quote: My sisters the swallows, it is now time for me also to speak, since you have already said enough.

stops.name: The Dalmatian coast, shipwrecked toward Syria
stops.campa: Burning to preach to the Saracens or die a martyr, Francesco takes ship from Ancona for Syria, and contrary winds throw the vessel onto the coast of Slavonia, the Dalmatian shore. No ship will sail east so late in the year. Penniless, he and his companion stow away aboard a boat bound back for Ancona; a stranger, the canon knows who sends such strangers, has secretly stocked food for them, which multiplies through the storm-lengthened crossing and feeds the whole crew. The first assault on the East ends where it began, but the vow holds.

stops.name: San Leo, the verse of the castle feast and the gift of La Verna
stops.campa: At the castle of San Leo in the Montefeltro, amid a great feast for a new knight, Francesco climbs onto a low wall and preaches on a verse of the troubadours he has made his own. Count Orlando Catani of Chiusi, pierced to the heart, draws him aside: he owns a mountain in Tuscany, La Verna, wild, solitary, fit for whoever would do penance far from the world, and he gives it to Francesco outright. Francesco sends two brothers to see it; they are met by fifty armed men against the wolves, and by falcons and a spring. The mountain waits eleven years for its wound.
stops.quote: So great is the good I have in sight, that every pain to me is a delight.
stops.quote_source: The First Consideration of the Holy Stigmata (appendix to the Fioretti)

stops.name: Santiago de Compostela, the houses through all the world
stops.campa: Turned toward Morocco and the Miramamolin to preach and be martyred, Francesco crosses Spain and comes as a pilgrim to the tomb of Saint James at Compostela. Praying there through the night, it is revealed to him that he is to take many more places for his brothers: that the Order must spread its houses through all the world. Sickness meets him on the road and forbids Morocco; he obeys the illness as a message and turns back through Spain to Italy, leaving the tradition of a first friary in the city of the Apostle.

stops.name: Rome, the Fourth Lateran Council: Francis and Dominic
stops.campa: Innocent III opens the greatest council of the age in the Lateran, and Francesco is in Rome as it decrees that no new religious rules be invented; his own brotherhood, already blessed by word of mouth, slips through the closing door of history. Here the tradition sets his meeting with Dominic of Caléruega: the Spaniard has seen in vision two men presented to Christ by the Virgin, and recognizing the beggar from the vision, embraces him. 'You are my companion; let us stand together, and no adversary will prevail.' The two orders are brothers from that embrace.

stops.name: Porziuncola, the Pentecost Chapter of the missions
stops.campa: At the Pentecost chapter of 1217 the brotherhood, grown past counting, divides the world like an inheritance. Provinces are drawn on the map of Christendom and beyond it: brothers to France, to Germany, to Hungary, to Spain, and across the sea to Syria under Brother Elias. Francesco himself sets out for France, land of his mother tongue of song, but at Florence Cardinal Ugolino, the Order's great protector and future Pope Gregory IX, turns him back: the head must not wander from the body. The Order becomes an army of the roads.

stops.name: Ancona, embarkation for the East
stops.campa: On the feast of Saint John the Baptist, Francesco sails at last from Ancona for the Crusade, with Peter Catani, Illuminato and a band of brothers. So many friars beg to go that he will not choose among them; he calls a child from the quay and lets the innocent finger pick the twelve who sail. The fleet runs by Cyprus to Acre, and from Acre down to the Nile, where the army of the Fifth Crusade lies rotting in its camp before Damietta. The little poor man goes to war carrying nothing.

stops.name: The camp before Damietta, the prophecy of defeat
stops.campa: In the crusader camp on the Nile, Francesco is shown the day's coming battle in prayer and is torn: if he speaks he will be called a fool, if he is silent his conscience will accuse him. He speaks. He walks the lines forbidding the attack in God's name; the barons laugh, the army advances on Damietta, and is cut to pieces, thousands of dead and captured by nightfall. Celano records the grief of the man of God over the slain, and the awe of an army that had laughed at him in the morning.
stops.quote: If the clash takes place today, the Lord has shown me that it will not go well for the Christians. But if I say so, they will call me a fool.

stops.name: Fariskur, the court of Sultan al-Kamil
stops.campa: During the truce Francesco and Brother Illuminato cross the lines toward the Saracen camp crying 'Soldan! Soldan!' They are seized, beaten, chained, and dragged before al-Malik al-Kamil, nephew of Saladin, who, expecting envoys or renegades, finds instead a small man in a patched habit offering to prove the Gospel by walking into fire with the sultan's own priests. The sultan will not light the fire, but he will not let him go: for days he keeps him, listening, and offers treasure that is refused. He sends him back with an escort, saying: 'Pray for me, that God may reveal to me the law most pleasing to Him.'
stops.quote: If you wish to be converted to Christ, you and your people, I shall most gladly stay with you for love of Him. But if you hesitate to abandon the law of Mohammed for the faith of Christ, then command that an enormous fire be lit, and I will enter the fire with your priests, that you may know which faith deserves to be held the holier and more certain.

stops.name: Damietta taken, the grief in the victory
stops.campa: Damietta falls in the night of 5 November, falls without a battle, because plague and famine have already killed the city; the crusaders climb the walls into streets carpeted with the dead. Then comes the sack. Francesco, who had crossed the world to save souls on both sides of the wall, watches Christians fight Christians over plunder amid the corpses of Saracens, and the canon records his sorrow and his departure. He turns his back on the victory and goes up to Acre and the holy places, until word from Italy calls him home to a house in disorder.
